Keywords: last click attribution last touch conversion credit default model channel credit
Description: 100% of conversion credit goes to the LAST channel the user clicked before converting. The default model in most platforms (GA4 pre-2023, Google Ads default).
Pros: businesses with simple funnels (one main channel)
Cons: Simple to understand. Easy to optimize toward. Works well for paid search where last click is usually strong intent.
Tool: Ignores all earlier touchpoints. Undervalues top-of-funnel channels (awareness ads, blog traffic, email nurture). Not accurate for complex, multi-session journeys.
column9: GA4, Google Ads (legacy default), most ad platforms

Keywords: first click attribution first touch awareness new customer acquisition top of funnel credit
Description: 100% credit goes to the FIRST channel a user touched before eventually converting. Emphasizes acquisition and awareness.
Best For: Understanding which channels first introduce users to your brand
Cons: Shows which channels introduce new customers. Good for measuring awareness campaign effectiveness.
Tool: Ignores everything that happened between first touch and conversion. Overvalues awareness channels. Not representative of conversion path complexity.

Keywords: linear attribution equal credit all touchpoints multi touch channel journey
Description: Equal credit distributed across ALL touchpoints in the conversion path. If 4 touchpoints, each gets 25%.
Best For: Businesses wanting to value all channels equally, reporting for stakeholders who want simplicity
Pros: Simple to explain. Acknowledges full journey. No single channel is over- or under-valued by design.
Cons: Equal credit isn't realistic — some touchpoints matter more than others. Hard to act on for budget optimization.

Keywords: time decay attribution recency recent touchpoints weighted most recent closer to conversion more credit
Description: Touchpoints closer in time to conversion receive more credit. A touchpoint 1 day before converts gets more credit than one 30 days before.
Best For: Short sales cycles, SaaS trials, e-commerce — where recency strongly correlates with intent
Pros: Reflects the reality that recent engagement often drives conversion. Good for optimizing bottom-of-funnel channels.
Cons: Undervalues awareness and research-phase channels. Not ideal for long B2B sales cycles where early touchpoints are just as critical.

Keywords: position based u-shaped attribution first last 40% middle 20% balanced
Description: 40% credit to the first touchpoint, 40% to the last touchpoint, 20% distributed equally across middle touchpoints. Balances acquisition and conversion.
Best For: Businesses that value both awareness (first touch) and conversion (last touch) in roughly equal measure
Pros: Acknowledges both the introduction (first) and the close (last). Doesn't ignore middle-funnel entirely.
Cons: The 40/40/20 split is arbitrary — not data-driven. Middle touchpoints still undervalued relative to their actual influence.

Keywords: data-driven attribution DDA machine learning google ads ga4 algorithmic conversion credit
Description: Uses machine learning to assign credit based on the actual contribution each touchpoint made to conversion probability. Compares converting vs non-converting paths.
Best For: Businesses with 300+ conversions/month, Google Ads campaigns, GA4 with sufficient data volume
Pros: Most accurate attribution model. Based on actual data from your specific customers. Continuously learns and improves. Google's recommended default.
Cons: Requires sufficient conversion volume (GA4: 400+ conversions in 28 days, Google Ads: 30+). Black-box model — hard to explain exactly how credit is assigned. Less actionable for small accounts.
Tool: GA4 (default for 400+ conversions), Google Ads, Adobe Analytics

Keywords: multi-touch attribution mta markov shapley algorithmic customer journey cross channel
Description: Advanced statistical models (Markov chains, Shapley values) to assign credit across ALL channels across the full customer journey, including cross-device and cross-channel.
Best For: Enterprise businesses with complex multi-channel funnels, significant ad budgets ($100K+/month), data science resources
Pros: Most complete picture of channel contribution. Cross-device tracking. Can include offline touchpoints. Scientific basis (Shapley = game theory).
Cons: Very expensive. Requires significant data volume and data science resources. Integration complexity across platforms. Privacy changes (iOS14+, cookie deprecation) reduce signal quality.
Tool: Northbeam, Triple Whale, Rockerbox, Measured, Nielsen

Keywords: media mix modeling mmm statistical regression incrementality causal inference top-down
Description: Statistical regression model that uses aggregate sales data, media spend, and external factors (seasonality, pricing) to estimate channel contribution — without cookies.
Best For: Enterprise brands with $1M+ annual ad spend, brands severely impacted by iOS14 privacy changes, companies with significant offline + online sales mix
Pros: Privacy-safe (doesn't require individual user tracking). Captures offline influence. Can include competitive spend
column9: Slow to run (weeks, not real-time). Expensive to build or buy. Low granularity (can't optimize individual ads). Requires long historical data (2+ years ideally).

Keywords: incrementality test lift study geo test holdout group true incremental impact causal
Description: Experimental methodology (A/B test at scale) to measure the TRUE incremental impact of a channel by comparing exposed vs unexposed groups. Gold standard for proving channel value.
Best For: Validating attribution models, measuring true ROI of a new channel, identifying over-credited channels
Pros: The most accurate way to measure true causal channel impact. Not affected by attribution model bias. Essential for budget decisions.
Cons: Expensive and time-consuming (geo tests need 4-8 weeks). Requires holding out budget during test (opportunity cost). Needs statistical expertise to design and interpret properly.
Tool: Google Geo Experiment, Meta Lift Tests, Measured.com
